question: Can a reinforcement-learning agent learn tactic choice, premise/term arguments, and backtracking jointly in HOL4 without training on human-written proof traces?

key_findings.claim: Representing a proof-search state as multiple alternative fringes makes backtracking a learned action rather than a fixed external search rule.
key_findings.evidence: Each fringe is an AND-set of remaining goals sufficient to finish one proof path, while the state retains all prior fringes as OR alternatives. A goal-value network scores and samples a fringe, so the agent can abandon a newly generated dead end and resume an older derivation.

key_findings.claim: The factorized policy makes a very large structured action space tractable enough for policy-gradient training.
key_findings.evidence: An action chooses fringe, first goal, one of the allowed tactics, and a sequence of theorem or term arguments. Separate goal and tactic networks plus an LSTM argument policy factorize its probability; the average theorem candidate set is 468 and a length-n argument list has nominal size 468^n.

key_findings.claim: Without human proof traces, TacticZero substantially outperforms random search on held-out HOL4 theorems and is close to the paper's hammer baseline.
key_findings.evidence: On a random 80/20 split of 1,342 provable core-library theorems and up to eight attempts per test theorem, it proves 62.3%, versus 14.2% for random rollouts and 64.5% for HOL(y)Hammer/Vampire. Theory-specific agents prove 81.7% of held-out set theorems, 61.7% of list theorems, and 75.0% of other theorems.

key_findings.claim: Argument selection is the most consequential learned component in the reported ablation.
key_findings.evidence: Freezing each module at its random initialization reduces training success, but disabling the recurrent argument policy causes the largest degradation; the remaining networks can partly compensate for a random fringe or tactic choice.

key_findings.claim: All discovered scripts are reconstructed and checked by HOL4, so search reward cannot substitute an invalid proof for a successful one.
key_findings.evidence: When an empty fringe is reached, the environment reconstructs a HOL4 proof script from the state sequence and sends it back to the kernel-backed prover for verification; the paper also prints multiple discovered scripts.

method.core_idea: Cast tactic-level interactive theorem proving as an episodic MDP whose policy controls both local proof steps and global choice among alternative partial derivations.
method.mechanism: Encode HOL4 expressions into 256-dimensional pretrained autoencoder representations; score fringes by summed goal values; sample tactics; recurrently select up to five prior theorems or goal terms as arguments; execute the action in HOL4; train all policies with REINFORCE, shaped progress rewards, and replay of the agent's recent successful proofs.
assumptions: The human-selected tactic vocabulary is expressive enough for every benchmark theorem.
Library order supplies an acceptable accessibility rule for premise candidates.
Summing independent goal logits is a useful proxy for the probability of completing an entire fringe.
Always tackling the first goal within a selected fringe loses little because all fringe goals must eventually be proved.
Shaped tactic rewards and difficulty-dependent terminal rewards preserve useful search behavior despite not being derived from proof cost.
A random held-out split within one curated HOL4 library measures the desired generalization.

techniques.role: Maintains an AND/OR proof-search structure inside the RL state.
Selects which partial derivation to extend or revisit.
Decomposes an enormous structured action into manageable conditional choices.
Models interaction and ordering among multiple tactic arguments.
Counteracts sparse rewards by revisiting self-discovered proofs that the stochastic policy forgets.
Turns proof completion into an exact, machine-checkable reward signal.

evaluations.setting: Random 80/20 split of 1,342 HOL4 core-library theorems
evaluations.metric: Percentage proved with at most eight attempts

evaluations.setting: Separate set, list, and other-theory 80/20 splits

evaluations.result: All learned modules help; the argument-policy freeze causes the largest visual drop
evaluations.baseline: Complete jointly trained agent and separate frozen goal/tactic policies

evaluations.result: Roughly two weeks for 800 iterations on one Tesla P100 plus one Xeon CPU; 50 HOL4 calls per episode and 0.1-second tactic timeout
evaluations.baseline: Not matched to competitor training cost

limitations: 'From scratch' means no human proof traces: the agent still relies on human-written theorem statements, library order, engineered tactics, prior lemmas, a pretrained expression autoencoder, HOL4's simplifier, and hand-designed rewards.
The benchmark is small, restricted to the subset known to be solvable by eight chosen tactics, and drawn from the same HOL4 core library used to define candidates.
Random theorem splitting can leak near-duplicate structure and prerequisite patterns; no chronological or novel-premise split stress-tests distribution shift.
The Hammer comparison is not budget- or premise-matched and the paper itself says direct comparison with TacticToe is impossible.
Reported pass rates use up to eight stochastic attempts without confidence intervals, multi-seed training statistics, or calibration against total inference compute.
REINFORCE plus ad hoc off-policy successful-proof replay has no stability analysis and costs about two weeks on the reported small task.
Fixed candidate lists cannot synthesize arbitrary new terms beyond variables present in the goal, limiting constructive mathematics.
failure_modes: Sparse terminal success prevents discovery of an initial proof and replay never activates.
The learned fringe score favors many individually easy subgoals whose conjunction is globally unproductive.
A needed premise is later in library order, outside the referenced theories, or absent from the candidate set.
The recurrent argument policy repeats or combines individually plausible lemmas into an ineffective list.
A stochastic policy reports high multi-attempt success but poor first-attempt reliability or excessive search cost.
Reward shaping encourages cheap local progress that expands the fringe and lengthens the eventual proof.
reusable_insights: Expose reversible search decisions to the policy when an environment can cheaply retain alternative partial states.
Factor tool actions into target, operation, and structured arguments while preserving their conditional dependence.
Use an exact verifier as the terminal learning signal and keep heuristic rewards auxiliary.
Evaluate proof agents by pass@k, first-attempt success, verifier calls, wall-clock, and training compute together.
Distinguish learning without proof demonstrations from learning without human-designed environments or curricula.
open_questions: Can value-guided AND/OR search or modern actor-critic methods improve sample efficiency over REINFORCE and replay?
How well does the policy transfer to new HOL4 theories, premises never used in training, longer proofs, or another proof assistant?
Can theorem generation, curriculum design, or intrinsic rewards supply useful tasks without a fixed human theorem corpus?
What benefit comes specifically from learned backtracking under matched search budgets against best-first, MCTS, and hypertree search?

competitive_landscape.title: TacticToe: Learning to Prove with Tactics
competitive_landscape.difference: TacticToe learns tactic guidance from recorded human HOL4 proofs and uses Monte Carlo tree search; TacticZero removes proof demonstrations and learns fringe selection jointly, but evaluates on a much smaller solvable subset.

competitive_landscape.title: HOList: An Environment for Machine Learning of Higher-Order Theorem Proving
competitive_landscape.relationship: contemporaneous higher-order RL environment and prover
competitive_landscape.difference: DeepHOL couples learned tactic/premise guidance to a fixed search loop and bootstraps from successful proof data in HOL Light; TacticZero explicitly parameterizes backtracking and trains all action levels in HOL4.

competitive_landscape.title: Generative Language Modeling for Automated Theorem Proving
competitive_landscape.difference: GPT-f trains a transformer on Metamath proof sequences and generates proof steps/terms; TacticZero avoids human proof traces but is constrained to a small tactic-and-candidate action space.

competitive_landscape.title: HyperTree Proof Search for Neural Theorem Proving
competitive_landscape.difference: HTPS represents proof obligations as a hypertree and uses AlphaZero-style online training with transformer policies across Metamath and Lean; TacticZero's earlier approach samples one fringe through a direct policy-gradient MDP.

competitive_landscape.title: LeanDojo: Theorem Proving with Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: later open benchmark and retrieval competitor
competitive_landscape.difference: LeanDojo scales to nearly 100,000 Lean theorems and evaluates a novel-premise split with explicit retrieval; TacticZero uses a 1,342-theorem HOL4 subset and a library-derived candidate pool.

novelty_assessment: The main novelty is the explicit fringe-set MDP that learns backtracking together with tactics and arguments while bootstrapping without human proof trajectories. The exact HOL4 verifier gives a strong learning signal, but the 'from scratch' label should be read narrowly and the small, tactic-filtered, randomly split benchmark does not establish broad mathematical autonomy. Later hypertree and retrieval-augmented systems provide stronger scaling and distribution-shift tests.
